In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

‘The Vaiont disaster was a complex landslide triggered by a combination of rainfall and reservoir level rise that developed over the period of 1 to 2 weeks in October 1963, and that was controlled by tectonic processes and the structural geology of the site.’
the Vaiont failure was a new, rather than a reactivated, landslide; it was not a failure of a clay seam; and it was not caused solely by the reservoir water level.

the landslide was triggered by a rainfall event, which caused failure in a pre-existing weak zone that was not at residual strength, and that failure occurred along a complex surface that was not a thin seam.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Vaiont failure is a large, complex and unique landslide that was initiated by the interaction of a number of factors, including rainfall, and developed by a combination of gravitational and hydrological mechanisms.

the 1963 Vaonit landslide was a large translational landslide that failed in response to the combined effects of the reservoir-induced pore pressure build-up in the landslide toe, the increased pore pressures induced by rainfall and the reduction in shear strength of the landslide mass due to the effects of rainfall.
the landslide was not an ancient re-activation of a slide mass, but rather an entirely new failure that was triggered by rainfall, and not by inundation of a slide toe.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the failure surface of the 1963 landslide was a single planar shear surface with an inclined top and a near horizontal base.
the landslide is not an ‘ancient’ reactivation, but is a new failure, which developed as a consequence of the reservoir inundation.
